Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a class cannot be certified under Rule 23(b)(3) where individual damages questions will overwhelm common questions.

Cite at least six decisions of the Seventh Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. Individual Damages Questions Predominate Over Any Common Questions, Defeating Certification Under Rule 23(b)(3).**

Rule 23(b)(3) permits certification only if "questions of law or fact common to class members predominate over any questions affecting only individual members." Fed. R. Civ. P. 23(b)(3). The predominance requirement is "far more demanding" than commonality, *Amchem Prods., Inc. v. Windsor*, 521 U.S. 591, 623-24 (1997), and the party seeking certification must affirmatively prove compliance with Rule 23 through evidentiary proof, not pleading allegations, *Comcast Corp. v. Behrend*, 569 U.S. 27, 33 (2013). A court must conduct a "rigorous analysis," even where that analysis overlaps with the merits. *Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Dukes*, 564 U.S. 338, 350-51 (2011); *Messner v. Northshore Univ. HealthSystem*, 669 F.3d 802, 811, 815 (7th Cir. 2012).

**A. Plaintiffs must show that damages can be measured on a classwide basis.**

Under *Comcast*, a damages model must measure only the damages attributable to the theory of liability on which the class is certified. 569 U.S. at 35. This Court has applied that principle. It recognizes that the need for some individualized damages inquiry does not by itself defeat certification, but it has been equally clear that the question is one of degree. Certification is improper where individual issues, including those bearing on injury and the amount of recovery, would consume the litigation and leave the common issues a minor part of it. *Butler v. Sears, Roebuck & Co.*, 727 F.3d 796, 801 (7th Cir. 2013); *Messner*, 669 F.3d at 815-17; *see also Mullins v. Direct Digital, LLC*, 795 F.3d 654, 671 (7th Cir. 2015) (recognizing that individualized damages do not defeat predominance where liability questions are common and the court can manage the remedial stage). Predominance therefore turns on whether the common questions drive the resolution of the case or whether the trial would break down into mini-trials. *Kleen Prods. LLC v. Int'l Paper Co.*, 831 F.3d 919, 925-28 (7th Cir. 2016); *Chi. Teachers Union, Local No. 1 v. Bd. of Educ.*, 797 F.3d 426, 444 (7th Cir. 2015).

**B. Here, damages turn on facts unique to each class member.**

This case falls on the side of the line that *Mullins* and *Messner* preserve. Plaintiffs' theory of liability may be stated in common terms, but the amount, and even the fact, of each member's loss depends on individual circumstances: [insert: what each member purchased or used, the price paid, the value received, and whether the member suffered any loss]. Plaintiffs offer no model that can resolve these variations with common proof. A model that assumes uniform loss across the class, without accounting for the differences described above, cannot satisfy *Comcast*. 569 U.S. at 35-38.

This Court has rejected certification on comparable showings. In *Parko v. Shell Oil Co.*, 739 F.3d 1083, 1085-86 (7th Cir. 2014), the Court recognized that where class members' claims vary in their circumstances and in the harm each allegedly suffered, a class action is not the superior or predominant mechanism for resolving them. In *Suchanek v. Sturm Foods, Inc.*, 764 F.3d 750, 759-61 (7th Cir. 2014), the Court vacated certification where individual questions of injury and recovery overshadowed the common questions. And in *Beaton v. SpeedyPC Software*, 907 F.3d 1018, 1025-29 (7th Cir. 2018), the Court reversed a certification order that did not give adequate weight to individualized questions bearing on class membership, injury, and relief.

**C. Bifurcation or issue certification cannot cure the problem.**

Plaintiffs may urge the Court to certify a liability-only class, or to defer damages to post-judgment proceedings. That approach does not satisfy Rule 23(b)(3) where the individualized inquiries are so extensive that the class device offers no efficiency. *Butler*, 727 F.3d at 800-02. Nor may Plaintiffs use "trial by formula" to avoid proving each member's entitlement. Defendant is entitled to litigate its defenses to individual claims. *Dukes*, 564 U.S. at 366-67. Where, as here, the issues that remain after resolving the common questions are the ones that determine whether and how much each member recovers, the common questions do not predominate. Certification should be denied or, on appeal, reversed.
